Good afternoon. I'm here to provide an overview of a comprehensive body of work that occurred across the organization
over the past 12 months to review and propose updates to the City's Corporate Policy Manual.
A corporate policy is created when Council's position on an issue should be part of a public record in keeping with open and accountable government.
Previously, Council had approved a master policy to govern the process, criteria and timely review of all corporate policies.
In keeping with the master policy, policy should be reviewed every three to five years for legislation changes, court decisions, council decisions, and new strategies, practices, and technologies.
The COVID-19 pandemic delayed policy reviews as staff prioritized the city's emergency response, so many were overdue for review.

Recognizing the delay, staff took a holistic approach and conducted a lean review, which found that the existing policy maintenance system and templates was manual, cumbersome, and less transparent to staff,
and the policy template was not user-friendly.
To improve the overall policy review process,
it is recommended that a new fillable form template be used,
that legislated services provide training to staff engaged in policy development,
and policy reviews be conducted through an equity-informed lens aimed to reduce barriers.
As well, authority to the clerk to make minor edits,
such as housekeeping changes to titles and language,
where the content of the policy is left unchanged, is recommended.

16 policies identified that required minor amendments and 22 recommending to be repealed,
which I will touch on further in the next few slides. A number of policies require major or
substantial revisions, which are not part of this report. This is the first of many corporate policy
reports as we strive to get back on track. The policies recommended for
amendment are contained in Appendix B to the staff report as both a clean copy

divisions responsible, job titles, and addressing a new hydro entity. And lastly
legislative changes clarify Council's role, address the special powers and

recommended to be repealed are contained as well in Appendix B to the staff
reports. Previously Council had supported a threshold to consider policy repeal on
four grounds noted on this slide here. There are six policies that are
recommended to repeal that pertain to programs or funding that no longer exist.
There are nine policies to repeal that pertain to regulations or legislation
already in place. There are three policies that conflict with another
policy and there are four policies that were found to be redundant or outdated.
It also came to staff's attention that there are policies arising from legislative amendments to the Municipal Act that were not adopted.
In accordance with Section 270 of the Act, the city is required to have a council and staff relations policy.
Policy provisions are not prescribed, and through internal discussions, it was noted that many policies are existing that govern how council and staff interact,
including the Code of Conduct, the city's procedure bylaw, the employee conflict of interest policy,
as well as policies required under the Occupational Health and Safety Act, amongst other legislation.
The proposed policy reiterates Council's commitment to those policies
and outlines existing mechanisms to address situations of non-compliance.
It models similar policies to the region of Waterloo, the town of Oakville, the city of Brampton, and the city of Oshawa.
And in accordance with Section 270 of the Act, the pregnancy and parental leave for members of Council also is required.

It did arise from work undertaken by former Kitchener Councillor Kelly Galloway-Sealock to advocate to the province to provide a clearer understanding of the legislative parameters for members of Council with respect to maternity and parental leave.

A pregnancy or parental leave for a member of Council is an absence of 20 consecutive weeks or less as a result of a member's pregnancy, the birth of a member's child, or the adoption of a child by the member in accordance with Section 259 of the Act.
Leaves longer than 20 weeks do still require Council authorization to prevent the seat from being declared vacant.
The policy recognizes a member's right of Council to take the leave for the member's pregnancy
and recommends that a standardized form be provided, which gives clarity for both parties
on which, if any, duties they would like to maintain while on that leave.
It does model the provisions in place at the City of Waterloo as well as the Town of Oakville.

policies highlighting some that require minor amendments and or those that are required
to be repealed.

Policy Manual provides consistent guidelines for the creation, management,
retention, and approval of corporate policies for the city that are publicly available.
